title: The Six-Month Gap: What Daylight Saving Quietly Costs an Interstate Freight Business
linkedin:
Clocks moved forward in New South Wales and Victoria last night. Queensland's didn't, because Queensland has never observed daylight saving.

That's not a trivia fact if you run freight between the two. For the next six months, a truck leaving a Brisbane depot and a dock expecting it in Sydney or Melbourne are reading from different clocks, and that one hour gap quietly reshapes scheduling for every interstate freight and logistics business on the east coast.

Here's the part that catches most operators out. Distribution centres book delivery windows in fifteen or thirty minute slots set against the local clock. A pickup time that landed neatly inside its Sydney booking window in September can now arrive an hour early or late, and tight dock schedules don't hold a slot open. The usual result is paid idle time at the gate, or a bump to the next window that pushes the rest of that day's run later.

None of this shows up as a missed delivery or a customer complaint. A driver waiting an hour at a gate is still being paid for that hour. A dispatcher rebuilding tomorrow's run because today's slipped is still spending time nobody budgeted for. Multiply that across every interstate crossing a fleet makes in a week, for six months running, and the cost sits quietly inside wages and overheads.

The gap isn't a one day inconvenience, it runs until the first Sunday in April. The businesses that handle it well rebuild the interstate schedule once, with the offset built into booking slots and driver start times from day one, rather than letting dispatch absorb the friction trip by trip.
